name: The theory of recollection (anamnesis)
plain_explanation: Plato argues that because we have ideas -- like 'exact equality' -- that we could never have gotten purely from imperfect sense experience, we must have known them before birth and simply be 'remembering' them; this is meant to prove the soul existed before the body.
precise_definition: The doctrine that all a priori knowledge (especially mathematical and logical concepts such as absolute equality, which is never actually found among sensible objects) is recollection of knowledge the soul possessed in a prior, disembodied existence, developed in the Phaedo and at greater length in the Meno via the interrogation of an untutored slave-boy about geometry.
why_it_mattered: It is Plato's central argument for the soul's pre-existence (half of the case for full immortality), and it later shaped rationalist views of innate ideas.
historical_origin: Presented in the Phaedo and elaborated in the Meno ('there is no teaching, but only recollection').
examples: We experience only approximate equality among sensible things, yet we understand 'absolute equality' -- which, Plato argues, we must have brought with us from a prior existence.
The Meno's slave-boy, questioned by Socrates about geometry, appears to 'remember' truths he was never taught.
objections: Russell: the argument is wholly inapplicable to empirical knowledge (the slave-boy could not 'remember' historical facts like the building of the Pyramids unless he had actually been present); Russell also doubts we truly possess an idea of 'absolute equality' at all, given that even the best modern measurement of a metre rod yields only an empirical, revisable claim, not certainty.

Even granting the idea exists, it is 'elicited by experience, although not directly derived from it,' and children do not possess it until a certain age; and if it were explained by a prior existence, the same problem simply recurs one step back, since that prior existence would need its own source for the idea.
influence_on_later_thinkers: A forerunner of later rationalist doctrines of innate ideas.
